title: Thermodynamics

notes.heading: 1. Zeroth & First Laws, Internal Energy & Mayer's Relation
notes.proseLatex: The Zeroth law defines temperature via transitive thermal equilibrium. In physics sign convention, First Law energy conservation reads $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ where $\Delta W = \int P\,dV$ is work done BY the system (area under $P$-$V$ curve; clockwise cycle gives $\Delta W > 0$ and $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$). For an ideal gas with $f$ degrees of freedom ($3$ monatomic, $5$ rigid diatomic), internal energy $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT = nC_V T$ is a pure state function of $T$, with $C_P - C_V = R$ and $\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$.

keyFormulas.label: First Law, Ideal Gas Internal Energy & Mayer's Relation
keyFormulas.latex: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \int P\,dV,\quad \Delta U = n C_V \Delta T = \frac{f}{2}nR\Delta T,\quad C_P - C_V = R,\quad \gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Distinguish path functions (Q, W) from state function U(T) and compute gamma.

examples.problemLatex: Find the fraction $\Delta W / \Delta Q$ when a rigid diatomic ideal gas expands isobarically.
stepsLatex: At constant pressure, $\Delta Q = nC_P\Delta T$ and $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$, so $\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \frac{C_V}{C_P} = 1 - \frac{1}{\gamma}$.
For a rigid diatomic gas ($f=5$), $\gamma = 7/5$, giving $\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \frac{5}{7} = \frac{2}{7}$.

notes.heading: 2. Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric & Isochoric Processes
notes.proseLatex: Isochoric ($\Delta V = 0 \implies W = 0,\; \Delta Q = \Delta U$); isobaric ($\Delta P = 0 \implies W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$). Isothermal ($\Delta T = 0 \implies \Delta U = 0$ for ideal gas) obeys $PV = \text{const}$ with $W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ and bulk modulus $K_T = P$. Reversible adiabatic ($\Delta Q = 0 \implies W = -\Delta U$) obeys $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$ (equivalently $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$ and $P^{1-\gamma}T^\gamma = \text{const}$) with steeper $P$-$V$ slope $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{ad}} = -\gamma\frac{P}{V} = \gamma\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}}$.

keyFormulas.label: Isothermal vs Adiabatic Work & Slope Ratio
keyFormulas.latex: $W_{\text{iso}} = nRT\ln\!\frac{V_2}{V_1},\quad W_{\text{ad}} = \frac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1},\quad \text{Slope}_{\text{ad}} = \gamma\,\text{Slope}_{\text{iso}}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute reversible isothermal/adiabatic work and identify steeper adiabats on PV plots.

notes.heading: 3. Second Law, Carnot Heat Engine & Refrigerator COP
notes.proseLatex: No cyclic engine converts heat $100\%$ into work (Kelvin-Planck) and heat never flows spontaneously from cold to hot without external work (Clausius). A reversible Carnot engine operating between hot reservoir $T_H$ and cold sink $T_C$ (in KELVIN!) achieves maximum theoretical efficiency $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = \frac{W}{Q_H}$, while a Carnot refrigerator has coefficient of performance $\text{COP} = \frac{Q_C}{W} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}$.

keyFormulas.label: Carnot Efficiency & Refrigerator COP
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Evaluate Carnot engine efficiency and refrigerator COP strictly in Kelvin.

examples.problemLatex: A Carnot engine operates between $127^\circ\text{C}$ and $27^\circ\text{C}$ absorbing $800\text{ J}$ per cycle. Find work output $W$.
stepsLatex: Convert to Kelvin: $T_H = 127 + 273 = 400\text{ K}$ and $T_C = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$.

wbjeebTraps: Physics vs Chemistry sign trap: physics uses $\Delta Q = \Delta U + W_{\text{by}}$ ($W>0$ in expansion), whereas chemistry writes $\Delta U = q + w_{\text{on}}$ ($w<0$ in expansion) — read carefully whether 'work done BY' or 'work done ON' the gas is asked!
Lowering sink temperature $T_C$ by $\Delta T$ boosts Carnot efficiency MORE than raising source temperature $T_H$ by the same $\Delta T$!

Free expansion into vacuum ($P_{\text{ext}} = 0$) is adiabatic with $Q = 0,\; W = 0,\; \Delta U = 0$, so an ideal gas suffers ZERO temperature change even though $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$ does NOT apply (irreversible!).
